title: FMLA, the Pregnant Workers Fairness Act and disability accommodation
summary: The federal leave and accommodation statutes that apply at 15 and 50 employees, and the North Carolina disability statute that runs alongside the ADA.

blocks.text: North Carolina has no state family or medical leave statute for private employers, so leave for a serious health condition, a new child or a family member's illness is governed by the federal Family and Medical Leave Act where it applies. The FMLA covers private employers with 50 or more employees for each working day during 20 or more calendar workweeks in the current or preceding year. An eligible employee must have 12 months of service and 1,250 hours in the prior 12 months, and must work at a site where the employer has 50 employees within 75 miles. Eligible employees receive up to 12 workweeks of unpaid, job-protected leave in a 12-month period for the listed reasons.

The Pregnant Workers Fairness Act applies to employers with 15 or more employees and requires reasonable accommodation of a qualified employee's or applicant's known limitations related to pregnancy, childbirth or related medical conditions, unless the accommodation would impose an undue hardship. A known limitation is a physical or mental condition the employee or a representative has communicated to the employer, whether or not it meets the ADA definition of disability. The ADA, also at 15 employees, requires reasonable accommodation of qualified individuals with disabilities and prohibits discrimination on the basis of disability.

items: The North Carolina Persons with Disabilities Protection Act makes it a discriminatory practice for an employer of 15 or more full-time employees in the State to refuse to hire, discharge or otherwise discriminate against a qualified person with a disability, and to require an applicant to identify as disabled before a conditional offer (G.S. 168A-5(a)).

The PWFA's qualified-employee definition is broader than the ADA's: an employee who temporarily cannot perform an essential function is still qualified if the function can be performed in the near future and the inability can be reasonably accommodated (42 U.S.C. § 2000gg(6)).
Under the FMLA, the 12-month service requirement need not be consecutive, and the 1,250 hours are hours actually worked (29 C.F.R. § 825.110).
An employer below 50 employees still faces accommodation duties at 15: unpaid leave can itself be a reasonable accommodation under the ADA or PWFA.

blocks.text: The common mistake at a 30-person employer is to tell a pregnant employee that the company is too small for maternity leave and has no obligation until she qualifies for the FMLA. The FMLA does not apply at 30 employees, but the PWFA and Title VII do at 15. A request for modified duties, extra breaks or time off for childbirth recovery is a request for accommodation of a known limitation, and refusing to engage is the violation.
